pink-squirrel:
How to tie a Pink Squirrel. John Bethke created this buggy nymph on Wisconsin's spring creeks, and the little pink collar seems to drive trout crazy. It works everywhere from the Driftless to the Rockies.

You'll need a scud or nymph hook, size twelve to eighteen. A gold bead. Black or pink eight-oh thread. A few strands of pearl Krystal Flash for the tail, red or gold wire for the rib, fox squirrel dubbing for the body, and pink UV chenille or Ice Dub for the collar.

Step one. Slide on the bead and start your thread. At the bend, tie in a short tail of pearl flash, then the wire.

Step two. Dub a buggy squirrel body two-thirds of the way up the shank, and rib it forward with the wire.

Step three. Right behind the bead, wrap two turns of pink chenille, or dub a small pink collar.

Step four. Pick out some fibers from the body for legs, and whip finish behind the bead.

Fish it under an indicator on spring creeks and tailwaters. The pink collar is the trigger.

egg-sucking-leech:
How to tie an Egg Sucking Leech. Black or purple with a bright egg at the head, this Alaskan classic looks like a leech raiding a salmon redd. Steelhead, salmon and big trout can't leave it alone.

You'll need a two-X-long streamer hook, size two to ten. Black six-oh thread. Black or purple marabou for the tail, black or purple chenille for the body, a black saddle hackle, and hot pink or orange chenille for the egg.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a marabou tail about as long as the hook shank.

Step two. Tie in a saddle hackle by its tip, and the body chenille, at the bend.

Step three. Wind the chenille forward to about a quarter shank behind the eye. Then palmer the hackle forward through it and tie it off.

Step four. In the space at the front, tie in the bright chenille and wind a fat little ball. That's the egg.

Step five. Whip finish in front of the egg.

Swing it for steelhead and salmon, or strip it for trout holding below spawning fish.

rainbow-warrior:
How to tie a Rainbow Warrior. Lance Egan's flashy little nymph glows over a red thread base. It doesn't copy any one bug, but on tailwaters it's one of the most reliable droppers you can tie on.

You'll need a curved nymph hook, size fourteen to twenty. A silver bead. Red eight-oh thread. Pheasant tail fibers for the tail, pearl tinsel for the body and wing case, and rainbow scud dubbing for the thorax.

Step one. Slide on the bead and start your red thread. Tie in a short tail of pheasant tail fibers and a strip of pearl tinsel at the bend.

Step two. Build a smooth, slightly tapered red thread body. Then pull the pearl tinsel forward over the top and tie it down, so the red shows through.

Step three. Dub a small thorax of rainbow scud dubbing behind the bead. Pull the pearl over it again as a wing case.

Step four. Tie it off and whip finish behind the bead.

Fish it as an attractor dropper in tailwaters and riffles, especially in clear water.

lightning-bug:
How to tie a Lightning Bug. A pearl or silver tinsel body gives this simple nymph a flash that looks like a mayfly nymph full of gas, getting ready to hatch. It's quick to tie, and a great dropper.

You'll need a nymph hook, size fourteen to twenty. A gold or silver bead. Black eight-oh thread. Pheasant tail fibers for the tail, pearl or silver tinsel for the body, and peacock herl or dubbing for the thorax with a flashback.

Step one. Slide on the bead, start the thread and tie in a short tail of pheasant tail fibers.

Step two. Tie in the tinsel and wrap a smooth, shiny body up to about two-thirds of the shank.

Step three. Tie in a strip of flash on top, wrap a peacock thorax, and pull the flash over the thorax as a flashback.

Step four. Tie it off and whip finish behind the bead.

Fish it as a dropper in clear water. The flash catches the light and draws strikes.

juju-baetis:
How to tie a Juju Baetis. Charlie Craven's slim, segmented nymph imitates the small blue-winged olive mayflies that hatch year-round. Two colors of thread twisted together give it a beautiful striped body.

You'll need a curved nymph hook, size eighteen to twenty-two. Olive and dark eight-oh threads. Brown fibers for the tail. Pearl flash and Thin Skin for the wing case, black dubbing for the thorax, and CDC or fibers for the legs.

Step one. Start the thread and tie in a short, sparse tail at the bend.

Step two. Twist two colors of thread together and wrap them up the shank, to make a slim, segmented abdomen.

Step three. Tie in the Thin Skin and pearl flash on top for the wing case, then dub a small black thorax.

Step four. Pull the wing case over the thorax, add a few fibers on each side as legs, and whip finish.

Fish it as the dropper before and during a blue-winged olive hatch.

scud:
How to tie a Scud. These little freshwater shrimp live in the weeds of spring creeks, tailwaters and lakes, and trout eat them all year. This simple pattern has a clear shellback and buggy legs.

You'll need a scud hook, size twelve to eighteen. A little lead-free wire for weight. Olive or tan eight-oh thread. A few short fibers for the tail. A strip of clear Scud Back, fine wire or mono for the rib, and olive, tan or pink dubbing.

Step one. Wrap a few turns of lead-free wire on the shank, then tie in a short tail at the bend.

Step two. Tie in the Scud Back strip and the rib at the bend.

Step three. Dub a full body forward to the eye. Then pick out the fibers underneath, so they look like legs.

Step four. Pull the shellback over the top and tie it off. Rib forward through it to make segments, and whip finish.

Fish it slowly near weed beds in spring creeks, tailwaters and lakes.

sow-bug:
How to tie a Sow Bug. Sow bugs are small, flat crustaceans that crawl through the weeds of spring creeks and tailwaters, and in some rivers trout eat more of them than anything else. This one is quick and simple.

You'll need a scud or nymph hook, size fourteen to eighteen. Grey eight-oh thread. Thin Skin or Scud Back for the back, fine wire for the rib, and grey rabbit or sow bug dubbing.

Step one. At the bend, tie in the back material and the fine wire.

Step two. Dub a broad, flat grey body up to the eye. Flatten it with your fingers if you need to.

Step three. Pull the back over, tie it off, and rib through it with the wire. Whip finish, then pick out the dubbing along the sides.

Dead-drift it near the bottom in spring creeks and tailwaters with weed beds.

kaufmanns-stone:
How to tie a Kaufmann's Stone. Randall Kaufmann's big stonefly nymph is realistic, with biot tails and antennae, a segmented back and three wing cases. It takes some time, but it's a fish catcher in big western rivers.

You'll need a three-X-long nymph hook, size four to ten. Lead-free wire for weight. Black six-oh thread. Black goose biots for the tail and antennae. Swiss straw or turkey for the back, mono or wire for the rib, black or brown seal-substitute dubbing, and turkey or Thin Skin for the wing cases.

Step one. Wrap lead-free wire along the shank and flatten it with pliers, so the nymph is wide and flat. Then tie in two biots at the bend as the tail.

Step two. Tie in the back material and the rib. Dub the abdomen, pull the back over it, and rib forward to make segments.

Step three. Build the thorax in three short sections. For each one, dub a little, then fold a wing case over the top.

Step four. Tie in two biots at the front as antennae, form a small head, and whip finish.

Fish it deep in fast western rivers before and during the salmonfly and golden stone hatches.

mercury-midge:
How to tie a Mercury Midge. Pat Dorsey's tiny pupa uses a silver-lined glass bead that looks just like the air bubble a midge carries as it rises to hatch. It's one of the simplest flies there is.

You'll need a curved midge hook, size eighteen to twenty-four. A silver-lined glass bead. Black eight-oh thread, and fine silver wire for the rib.

Step one. Slide the glass bead onto the hook, and start the thread behind it.

Step two. Tie in the wire, wrap a slim thread body down into the bend and back, then rib it with the wire in even turns.

Step three. Tie off the wire and whip finish right behind the bead.

Fish it near the surface or at mid-depth when midges are hatching, often below a small dry.

wd-40:
How to tie a WD-40. Mark Engler's little tailwater fly passes for an emerging midge or a tiny mayfly nymph. It uses one bunch of wood duck fibers for both the tail and the wing case, so it's quick to tie in small sizes.

You'll need a curved midge hook, size eighteen to twenty-four. Olive or grey eight-oh thread. Wood duck or mallard flank fibers for the tail and wing case, and muskrat or another fine dubbing for the thorax.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a few wood duck fibers as a short tail. Don't trim the butts. You'll use them later.

Step two. Wrap the thread over the butts to make a slim, tapered abdomen.

Step three. Dub a small thorax, then pull the fiber butts over the top as a wing case and tie them down.

Step four. Trim the excess and whip finish.

Fish it as a dropper in tailwaters. It's very effective in winter.
